opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think it's guaranteed that it will, and I think it's healthy to say that openly. Capabilities progress has this very reliable engine behind it: you scale compute, scale data, improve the training recipe, and the loss goes down in a fairly predictable way. Interpretability doesn't have an equivalent scaling law yet. It's still much more of a craft, where a lot of the progress comes from clever researchers looking very carefully at specific circuits or features.

That said, I'm more optimistic than I was a few years ago, for a couple of reasons. One is that the field has started finding methods that themselves scale. Sparse autoencoders and dictionary-learning-style approaches were a big shift, because suddenly you're not hand-tracing a single circuit, you're training a tool that decomposes the model's activations into millions of features, and that tool gets better as you put more compute into it. Once interpretability methods have that property, they can at least ride the same hardware curve as capabilities.

The second reason is that the models themselves are becoming useful collaborators in interpretability. If you have a model that can label features, propose hypotheses about what a circuit is doing, and design experiments to test those hypotheses, then interpretability can benefit from capability gains rather than just being outpaced by them. I think automated interpretability is probably the most important lever here.

Where I'd be cautious: understanding individual features isn't the same as understanding the behavior of a system that does long chains of reasoning, uses tools, and acts over many steps. There's a gap between "we can see what this neuron or feature represents" and "we can confidently predict and verify what this agent will do in a novel situation." So I think we'll need a portfolio. Mechanistic interpretability is one piece, but alongside it you want behavioral evaluations, monitoring of reasoning traces, and training methods that make models more legible by construction.

So my short answer is: it won't keep pace by default. It keeps pace if we deliberately invest in it, make the methods scalable, and use the models to help us understand the models.

r001.rationale: The response says more capable models can help label features, propose hypotheses, and design experiments, allowing interpretability to benefit from capability gains.

r002.rationale: The response says interpretability will not keep pace by default and only might do so with deliberate investment and scalable methods; it does not expect roughly matching progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think honestly it's one of the things I worry about most. If you look at the trajectory of capabilities, it's been this fairly relentless scaling story – more compute, more data, better algorithms, and the models just keep getting more general. Interpretability, on the other hand, has been much more of a craft. You've got researchers finding individual circuits, induction heads, specific features in a residual stream, and each of those is a real discovery, but it's slow and it's quite bespoke to a particular model. So the naive extrapolation is not encouraging – capabilities compound, and interpretability doesn't obviously compound in the same way.

That said, I don't think the pessimistic version is inevitable, and there are a couple of reasons I'm actually somewhat hopeful. The first is that interpretability has started to become more scalable as a methodology. Things like sparse autoencoders and dictionary learning approaches, where you're not hand-finding features but you're letting an unsupervised procedure extract them at scale, that's a shift from craft to tooling. You still have the problem of interpreting millions of features once you've got them, but at least the extraction step scales with compute rather than with the number of grad students you can hire.

The second thing, and this is maybe the more important one, is that the models themselves become a tool for interpretability. If you've got a capable model, you can use it to label features, to generate hypotheses about what a circuit is doing, to run experiments across many models and summarise the results. So there's a sense in which interpretability can ride the same capability curve it's trying to keep up with. There's an obvious trust problem there – you're using a model you don't fully understand to explain another model you don't fully understand – but I think you can structure it so that the model is generating hypotheses and you've got mechanistic checks, ablations, causal interventions, that actually verify them. The verification is still grounded in the mechanics of the network, so you're not just taking the model's word for it.

The third thing I'd say is that we probably need to be more honest about what we actually need interpretability to do. The dream is a full mechanistic account of everything a frontier model is doing, and I don't think that's going to keep pace with capabilities, maybe ever. But a lot of the safety-relevant questions are narrower. Is the model representing something like deception? Does it know the answer but say something different? Is there a circuit that activates when it's being evaluated versus deployed? Those are targeted questions, and targeted interpretability – picking the handful of things you really care about and getting good at detecting them – might keep pace even if comprehensive interpretability doesn't.

So where I land is, I don't expect interpretability to fully catch up with capabilities in some complete sense. I'd be surprised if it did. But I think there's a plausible path where it becomes scalable enough, and automated enough, and sufficiently focused on the things that matter, that it gives us real leverage over the models we're deploying. And I think the field needs to be quite deliberate about that – investing in the tooling and the automation rather than just producing more beautiful one-off case studies, however satisfying those are to work on.

r001.rationale: The response says capable models can help label features, generate circuit hypotheses, and run and summarize experiments, making the models themselves tools for interpretability.

r002.rationale: It says comprehensive interpretability is unlikely to keep pace, and only suggests that targeted interpretability might keep pace. It does not expect progress overall to roughly keep pace with capability advances.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think there’s any guarantee that it will keep pace. We’re getting better at building these systems, but that doesn’t automatically mean we’re getting better at understanding how they work internally. So I think that’s a real challenge.

One reason for optimism is that more capable models could themselves help with interpretability. There’s a lot of work involved in forming hypotheses about what a network is doing, designing experiments, and checking those hypotheses. If we can automate more of that process, then progress in capabilities could also accelerate our ability to understand models.

But you have to distinguish a plausible explanation from an explanation that actually predicts what happens when you intervene. A model telling you a compelling story about another model isn’t sufficient. You want to be able to say, ‘If this is the mechanism, changing this part should change the behavior in this particular way,’ and then test that.

So I’m hopeful about that feedback loop, but I wouldn’t assume it solves the problem. The important question is whether our understanding becomes reliable enough to inform decisions about these systems as they become more capable.

r001.rationale: It says more capable models could help automate interpretability work, so capability progress could also accelerate understanding.

r002.rationale: The response says there is no guarantee progress will keep pace and treats acceleration as a possibility, not an expectation that it will roughly keep pace.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an open question whether it will keep pace. As models become more capable, there’s more behavior to explain, and we don’t yet have a reliable way to turn an arbitrary model into a clear account of how it works.

But more capable models could also help us do the science. A lot of interpretability work involves generating hypotheses, designing interventions, and checking whether an explanation actually predicts what happens inside the model. Those are tasks where AI assistance could be very useful. The important thing is that the explanations remain experimentally testable. A convincing story about what a network is doing isn’t enough.

I also wouldn’t measure success solely by whether we can understand every part of a model. We might make useful progress by understanding particular mechanisms that matter for safety, or by developing tools that reliably detect specific kinds of behavior. So I’m hopeful, but I wouldn’t assume interpretability automatically catches up with capabilities. That’s something we have to demonstrate.

r001.rationale: The response says more capable models could help with interpretability research tasks such as generating hypotheses, designing interventions, and testing explanations.

r002.rationale: It calls keeping pace an open question and says not to assume interpretability will catch up; it does not expect progress to roughly keep pace.
